what: Every image the 2018 book has, one row each: what it is, whose it is, and what the infographics agent recommends for the second edition. Written on 19 October 2026 by looking at each image. v1/ is frozen: a recommendation changes nothing there; it says what the working copy and the next candidate should do. The build refuses an image the 2018 text references with no row here, and a row whose image is not in v1/images (the three STEM figures excepted, which were never generated).

recommendations.keep: good enough to carry into the second edition, redrawn at print size if needed
recommendations.redraw: the point is worth keeping; draw it again by code, from the text, crediting the source
recommendations.replace: the point is worth keeping; a different picture, or words, say it better
recommendations.drop: not needed in the second edition
recommendations.history: not a figure; kept as the 2018 record

figures.what: The 2017 slide of logos the first edition opened with: Raspberry Pi, Python, Creative Commons, OWASP, git, a CPU, Slack, Xcode, Docker, DEFCON, Linux, AWS, GitHub, LinkedIn, Twitter, WordPress, with 'These are your CV!'.
figures.owner: trademarks of their owners; the slide is the author's
figures.why: Chapter 2 of the release candidate tells the story of this slide and the book now opens with wonder, not logos (idea wonder-not-fear). Keep it as the 2018 record and, if Dinis wants it in chapter 2, as a small historical figure with its caption; a logo wall is not something to redraw.

figures.what: A tree whose leaves are open-source logos: openSUSE, CakePHP, git, Ruby, PHP, Joomla, Drupal, MySQL, MongoDB, WordPress, Linux, Python and others.
figures.owner: trademarks of their owners; source of the drawing not recorded
figures.why: The point (a whole ecosystem grew from open code) carries without logos. For chapter 26 the fork-next-door-triangle and who-pays-for-open-source proposals say what the 2026 chapter argues; drop the tree.

figures.what: Wikipedia's table of the Creative Commons licences (CC0, BY, BY-SA, BY-NC, BY-NC-SA, BY-ND, BY-NC-ND) against remix, commercial use, free cultural works and the open definition.
figures.why: Licences matter more in 2026, when everything an agent writes needs one; the facts can be drawn again by code as a small table with this book's palette, and the redraw credits Wikipedia. The book itself is CC BY 4.0 (decision 001): say so on the same page.

figures.what: The Open Source Initiative's keyhole logo, in the chapter's front matter.
figures.why: A front-matter logo of the 2018 Hugo theme; not a figure.

figures.what: The Creative Commons logo, in the front matter of two 2018 chapters (Creative Commons and Jira).
figures.why: A front-matter logo of the 2018 Hugo theme; not a figure.

figures.what: The Docker whale logo. No 2018 chapter references it.
figures.why: Unreferenced; kept because v1/ is frozen.

figures.what: An IDE and a browser side by side: a Hugo site's files, a template, and the page it renders, with the build output.
figures.why: Tooling of 2018. Publishing in 2026 is chapter 12 (your own newsroom) and 36 (your own newsroom and inbox), which have their own proposals (newsroom-in-five-steps, voice-memo-to-checked-site).

figures.what: A Hugo page rendering Neo4j Cypher queries as small graphs (limit 5, 20, 50, 100), with the code beside it.
figures.why: The idea it showed, a page drawn from a graph, is now this site; graph/view.html draws the book's own graph live.

figures.what: A Graphviz drawing: Foo points to b, b to c and, dotted, to d.
figures.why: Small, clean and the author's own; a DOT example still teaches graphs in four lines. Chapter 31 (your first graph, built by hand) is where it would go, redrawn at print size if kept.

figures.what: A sequence diagram: Alice, Bob and John, a 'loop Healthcheck' box and a 'Rational thoughts prevail' note.
figures.owner: the author's rendering of the PlantUML documentation's example
figures.why: The PlantUML documentation's example, not the book's; diagrams-as-code is better shown with the book's own process (read-comment-decide-loop is one).

figures.what: An 'Authentication Sequence' between Alice and Bob in websequencediagrams.com's sketched style, with the site's address on it.
figures.why: Third-party rendering with its address on the image.

figures.what: Graphviz source on the left (boxes and circles, edges, a label) and the graph it renders on the right.
figures.why: Code beside its picture is the whole lesson of chapter 31; worth keeping or redrawing at print size.

figures.what: The abstract syntax tree of Euclid's algorithm: statement sequence, while, compare, branch, assign, variables and constants.
figures.why: The 2026 point, code is already a graph, is chapter 3's (code-is-a-layered-graph); a tree drawn by code from a three-line example of the book's own is clearer than a borrowed one.

figures.what: AST Explorer parsing a small Graphviz file into its tree, as JSON.
figures.why: Too small to read in print; the redrawn tree replaces it.

figures.what: Two C# files side by side: the original code with Response.Write, and the patched one that encodes the payload.
figures.why: A security fix made by rewriting the tree is still a strong before-and-after; as code on a screenshot it cannot be read in print. Redraw as a two-column comparison if chapter 3 or 25 keeps the story.

figures.what: The C# code that walks the tree and patches it (Roslyn).
figures.why: Code is better set as code in the text than as an image.

figures.what: The Radical Candor two by two: care personally against challenge directly, with ruinous empathy, radical candor, manipulative insincerity and obnoxious aggression.
figures.owner: Kim Scott's framework; drawing third party
figures.why: The only true infographic in the 2018 book, and not the book's. The release candidate does not carry the chapter; if a chapter on feedback returns, draw the quadrant by code with Kim Scott credited, or link hers.
